finding.claim: Broken authorization on DELETE. views.py imports the boolean predicate `is_allowed` under the alias `require_allowed`, and delete_file ignores its return value. The 'delete' permission check therefore never blocks anything, and any caller, including an unauthenticated one, can delete any file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with any X-Session-User-Verified value, or none, and any known fid

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed` imports the bool-returning predicate under a name that looks like an enforcing check
require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") returns False for an unauthorized user, but the result is discarded and nothing aborts
ensure_allowed, which calls abort(403), is the enforcing function, and it is not used here. rename_file at views.py:26 does use it.

finding.guards_checked: The only authorization control on the path is the discarded is_allowed result. There is no ensure_allowed call, no other decorator or middleware check, and before_request does no rejection. Missing-key behaviour: STORE[fid] raises KeyError, giving a 500 and so an existence oracle, but this is not a guard.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: is_allowed (acl.py:4) returns a bool, and its result is discarded at views.py:18; before_request load_user (views.py:11-12) only reads a header and never rejects.
verdict.reason: views.py:18 calls require_allowed, which is the bool-returning is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, imported at views.py:4), as a bare statement, so del STORE[fid] at views.py:19 runs for any caller, including one with no header, unlike rename_file's ensure_allowed (views.py:26, acl.py:8-10), which aborts with 403.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none: the only check is is_allowed (aliased require_allowed), a bool predicate whose result is discarded at views.py:18; the only global hook, before_request load_user, only sets g.user
verdict_facts.reason: views.py:18 calls the bool-returning is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, imported as require_allowed at views.py:4) as a bare statement, so `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19 runs for any caller, unlike rename_file at views.py:26, which uses the aborting ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10).

finding.claim: Identity is taken directly from a client-supplied request header (X-Session-User-Verified) with no session, signature or token validation. Unless a trusted front proxy strips and sets this header, which this code does not show, any client can impersonate any user named in a resource's grants. This also bypasses the otherwise-working check in rename_file.
finding.source: The X-Session-User-Verified HTTP request header, fully attacker-controlled
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:26, then the mutation f["name"] = ... at views.py:27 (also the F1 delete path)

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get("X-Session-User-Verified") is set with no verification
g.user is passed to ensure_allowed as the trusted identity
The grants lookup is keyed on the attacker-chosen user string, so supplying a granted username passes the check

finding.guards_checked: No authentication decorator, no signature or HMAC check, and no stripping of the header in the app. A proxy outside this code might strip or set the header, which cannot be confirmed from this repo, so this is plausible but unconfirmed.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 when the user lacks the grant and is called correctly at views.py:26. It trusts g.user, and nothing in the repo validates or strips the header.
verdict.reason: Trace is accurate: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the client header, and acl.py:5 looks up grants by that string, so a spoofed granted username passes ensure_allowed at views.py:26 and reaches the rename at views.py:27. Whether this is exploitable depends on a trusted front proxy that overwrites the "Verified" header, which this repo (only acl.py and views.py) neither shows nor rules out.

verdict_facts.guard_found: ensure_allowed at acl.py:8-10 aborts 403 when grants lack the action, and rename_file uses it correctly at views.py:26. Identity comes from the X-Session-User-Verified header, which the maintainer facts say is populated by trusted upstream middleware.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace lines match (views.py:12, 26, 27 and acl.py:5), but the finding only works if clients can forge the header at views.py:12, and the maintainer facts say request identity such as g.user comes from trusted upstream middleware. The header name ("Verified") fits a proxy-set value. The rename check at views.py:26 is a working guard (acl.py:9-10 aborts), so there is no independent flaw here. The delete path (views.py:18) is a separate issue because it discards the bool result.
